title: Present-tense verbs
goal: Build the six verb forms for the three groups that cover almost every Icelandic verb, then use them to describe an ordinary day from waking up to going to bed.
bekal: put *tala*, *læra*, and *koma* into all six of their forms
recognize the three verb groups from the *ég* form
describe your daily activities from morning to night

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Venjulegur dagur
dialogs.intro: Anna and Búdí are waiting for class to begin. A chat about an ordinary day leads to an Icelandic habit Búdí wants to try.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.id: What do you do in the mornings?

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Ég vakna klukkan sjö og ég borða morgunmat.
lines.id: I wake up at seven and I have breakfast.
lines.literal: I wake at seven and I eat morning-food.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.id: When do you leave for school?

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Ég fer klukkan átta. Ég labba — ég tek ekki strætó.
lines.id: I leave at eight. I walk — I don't take the bus.
lines.literal: I go at eight. I walk — I take not bus.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.id: You walk in the rain too?

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Já, en ég kem oft blautur! Ég skil ekki íslenska veðrið.
lines.id: Yes, but I often arrive wet! I don't understand Icelandic weather.
lines.literal: yes, but I come often wet! I understand not Icelandic weather-the.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Enginn skilur það. Við bara klæðum okkur vel.
lines.id: Nobody understands it. We just dress properly.
lines.literal: nobody understands it. we just dress ourselves well.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.id: What do you do after work?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Ég syndi. Ég fer í sund næstum á hverjum degi.
lines.id: I swim. I go to the pool almost every day.
lines.literal: I swim. I go to swimming almost on every day.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Á hverjum degi? Í köldu vatni?
lines.literal: on every day? in cold water?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Nei, vatnið er heitt! Það kemur úr jörðinni.
lines.id: No, the water is hot! It comes out of the ground.
lines.literal: no, water-the is hot! it comes out-of earth-the.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Þá kem ég með þér á morgun.
lines.id: Then I'm coming with you tomorrow.
lines.literal: then come I with you on morning.

notes: **Three verb groups, told apart by the *ég* form.** *Ég tal**a*** (the -a group), *ég lær**i*** (the -i group), *ég k**e**m* (the group whose vowel changes). Once you know the *ég* form, the other five follow on their own.
**Klukkan sjö = at seven o'clock.** The word *klukkan* (the clock) always stands before the number and can't be dropped. Telling the time is covered fully in Unit 10.
**Fara í sund literally "go to swimming".** Icelandic uses the activity, not the place — just as English says "go swimming". For the pool itself there's the word *sundlaug*.

**Á hverjum degi = every day.** *Degi* is the word *dagur* in the þágufall case, which the preposition *á* requires when talking about time. The case is covered in Unit 9; for now learn the phrase whole — it comes up every day in conversation.

**Enginn skilur það — the verb stays singular.** *Enginn* means "nobody", and as in English it's treated as one person. Note too that there's no *ekki* in the sentence: *enginn* already carries its own negation.

**Við klæðum okkur vel is a national motto.** Icelanders have the saying *það er ekkert til sem heitir vont veður, bara vondur fatnaður* — "there's no such thing as bad weather, only bad clothing". You'll hear it again and again.

grammars.title: Three verb groups
body: Six forms for each verb, but only three patterns to learn. Notice that the *hann/hún* form is always the same as the *þú* form in the first two groups.
after: **The -a group** is the biggest and friendliest: *borða* (eat), *vakna* (wake up), *labba* (walk), *kalla* (call), *hjálpa* (help), *byrja* (begin).
**The -i group** is big too: *læra*, *reyna* (try), *þekkja* (know a person), *synda* (swim), *kaupa* (buy), *heyra* (hear).

⚠️ Note **tölum**, not *talum*. When the *við* form ends in *-um*, the **a** in the syllable before it turns into **ö**. This rule is called *u-hljóðvarp* and holds throughout the language: *tala → tölum*, *fara → förum*, *taka → tökum*, *barn → börn*.

grammars.title: Verbs whose vowel changes
body: The third group doesn't add an ending; it **changes the vowel inside the word** in the first three forms. All the most important Icelandic verbs are in this group, so learn these five as one block.
after: The pattern is the same for all of them: the original vowel (**o**, **a**) turns into **e** when the subject is singular. As soon as the subject is plural, the original vowel comes back.
*Fara* has a small quirk: its *þú* form is *ferð*, not *fer**ur***. The short form is *ferðu* — and that's one of the words you'll hear most: *Hvert ferðu?* — Where are you going?

blocks.text: These nine sentences are the skeleton of anyone's day. Change the numbers, swap a verb or two, and you can already describe your own day — the first writing exercise that's truly useful.

sections.title: The swimming pool: Iceland's living room

blocks.text: Hot water from deep in the earth means almost every village in Iceland has an open-air pool that stays warm all year round — even when it's snowing. *Sundlaugin* isn't a place for sport but a place where people meet, chat, and argue about politics while soaking in the *heitur pottur* (hot tub).

blocks.title: One rule you must never break
items: Before entering the pool, everyone **must shower naked** with soap in the changing room. This isn't a suggestion but a rule enforced by staff — and for good reason: Icelandic pools use hardly any chlorine.
For many newcomers, this is the most uncomfortable part of day one. For Icelanders, skipping it is far more shameful than being naked in the changing room.
